label: Encouraging Others
framing: Encouragement is not flattery but the steady gift of telling someone the truth that holds them up. Scripture treats it as a real ministry, a thing the body of Christ owes one another daily, because the discouraged heart cannot always carry itself and was never meant to.
cultural: We are quick to criticize and slow to bless, fluent in what is wrong with a person and shy about what is good in them. The internet has made the cutting word cheap and the kind one rare. The Bible reverses this, weighting its commands toward building up rather than tearing down, and naming the well-timed word a thing of beauty and even of power.
historical: The early church gave one of its own the name Barnabas, son of encouragement, because that was what he did, taking in the feared Saul when no one else would and later restoring the failed young Mark. From Paul's letters, written to keep small frightened churches standing, to the long Christian habit of bearing one another's burdens, the church has known it survives on this ordinary grace.
application: Say the good thing out loud, today, since the encouragement you keep inside helps no one. Be specific, naming what you actually see in a person rather than offering a vague compliment. Go to the discouraged before they ask, for the lonely rarely do. And aim your words at who they are becoming in Christ, which is the truest and most lifting thing you can ever tell them.

verses.text: Therefore encourage and build one another up, just as you are already doing.
verses.where: After reminding the church that God appointed them to salvation, not wrath, Paul tells them to encourage and build one another up, just as they are already doing. The site's plain note asks whom you could encourage and build up this week. Paul commands what they already practise, so that they keep doing it.

verses.text: But exhort one another daily, as long as it is called today, so that none of you may be hardened by sin’s deceitfulness.
verses.where: The letter tells believers to exhort one another daily, as long as it is called today, so that none of them is hardened by sin's deceitfulness. The site's note says the today of the psalm now names the whole present time as a season of opportunity, and the plain note says holding on is something believers do together. It asks who knows you well enough to notice if you were growing cold.

verses.text: Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus, whom the apostles called Barnabas (meaning Son of Encouragement), sold a field he owned, brought the money, and laid it at the apostles’ feet.
verses.where: Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus, is called Barnabas by the apostles, which means Son of Encouragement, and he sells a field and lays the money at their feet. The site's plain note says the sharing was free and generous, not forced, and that Barnabas is named because his gift was worth noticing. Encouragement in Acts begins with an open hand.

verses.text: When Saul arrived in Jerusalem, he tried to join the disciples, but they were all afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple. Then Barnabas brought him to the apostles and described how Saul had seen the Lord, who spoke to him on the road to Damascus, and how Saul had spoken boldly in that city in the name of Jesus.
verses.where: When Saul tries to join the disciples in Jerusalem they are all afraid of him, and Barnabas brings him to the apostles and tells them how Saul saw the Lord and spoke boldly in Damascus. The site's plain note says every changed person needs a Barnabas, someone who will stand next to them while others are still afraid. Sometimes encouragement means vouching for someone.

verses.text: Anxiety weighs down the heart of a man, but a good word cheers it up.
verses.where: Anxiety weighs down the heart of a man, but a good word cheers it up. The site's note sets it in a chapter whose sayings are above all about words: rash speech that wounds and wise speech that heals. A sentence costs little, and it can lift a weight.

verses.text: Strengthen the limp hands and steady the feeble knees! Say to those with anxious hearts: “Be strong, do not fear! Behold, your God will come with vengeance. With divine retribution He will come to save you.”
verses.where: Isaiah tells God's people to strengthen limp hands and steady feeble knees, and to say to the anxious, be strong, do not fear, your God will come to save you. The site's note on the chapter says the fearful are told to be strong because God is coming to save. Biblical encouragement points past the speaker to what God will do.

verses.text: Let no unwholesome talk come out of your mouths, but only what is helpful for building up the one in need and bringing grace to those who listen.
verses.where: Paul tells believers to let no unwholesome talk come out of their mouths, only what helps build up the one in need and gives grace to those who listen. The site's note on the chapter lists words that build up among the marks of the new self. The plain note asks whether our words this week have built people up or torn them down.

verses.text: But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the arrival of Titus, and not only by his arrival, but also by the comfort he had received from you. He told us about your longing, your mourning, and your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced all the more.
verses.where: Pressed by conflicts outside and fears within, Paul says God, who comforts the downcast, comforted him by the arrival of Titus and the good news he brought. The site's plain note asks whom God has used to comfort you, often without their knowing it, and notices that if you are among the downcast, Paul was too. Even an apostle needed someone to arrive.

verses.text: For I long to see you so that I may impart to you some spiritual gift to strengthen you, that is, that you and I may be mutually encouraged by each other’s faith.
verses.where: Paul says he longs to see the Roman believers to strengthen them, and then restates it: that he and they may be mutually encouraged by each other's faith. The site's note says the apostle expects to receive as well as give. Encouragement runs both ways.

verses.text: May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, because he has often refreshed me and was unashamed of my chains. Indeed, when he arrived in Rome, he searched diligently until he found me.
verses.where: Writing from prison after many in Asia deserted him, Paul says Onesiphorus often refreshed him, was not ashamed of his chains, and searched Rome until he found him. The site's plain note asks who is in a hard place that others keep away from, and whether you could be the one who finds them. Sometimes the encouragement is simply arriving.

misread.taken: Let us not neglect meeting together is used to shame people who have stopped coming to church, including those who were hurt there, as if the verse were a rule about attendance.
misread.says: The site's plain note says the verse is a call to encouragement, not a club. It was written to weary believers who were drifting away, to call them back to people who would help them hold on, and it is never a reason to shame someone who has stepped away from a place where they were harmed, or to force anyone back into danger. Its own command is to consider how to spur one another on to love and good deeds.
misread.text: And let us consider how to spur one another on to love and good deeds. Let us not neglect meeting together, as some have made a habit, but let us encourage one another, and all the more as you see the Day approaching.

whole: Many people go weeks without anyone saying a kind and true word to them. A carer finishes a long day nobody noticed; a young father wonders whether he is doing anything right; a teenager hears mostly what he got wrong; a pastor hears every complaint and few thanks. Others want to encourage and do not know how. They fear sounding false, or they wait for a big moment and miss the small ones, or they say only that it will be fine, which rarely helps.

Scripture treats encouragement as something believers owe one another daily, not an extra kindness. The letter to the Hebrews tells them to exhort one another every day while it is still today, so that none is hardened, and the site's plain note says holding on is something believers do together. Proverbs observes that anxiety weighs the heart down and a good word cheers it. Even Paul, an apostle, says he was downcast and that God comforted him by the arrival of Titus. Part of why we fail to encourage is that we are busy, part is that we assume it is someone else's job, and part is a quiet reluctance to praise another person at all. Most of us have been carried by a word someone did not have to say, and have kept back words we should have said.

So the Bible's wisdom is specific. Barnabas, the Son of Encouragement, gave freely, and later stood beside Saul when the whole church was afraid of him; encouragement sometimes means vouching for someone others will not yet trust. Paul tells the Ephesians to say what builds up the one in need, which means paying attention to what that person needs, not to what we would like to say. Isaiah's command is to strengthen limp hands and tell anxious hearts that God will come, so encouragement points past the speaker to God. Onesiphorus searched Rome until he found Paul in prison; sometimes the encouragement is simply turning up. And encouragement is not flattery, or silence about wrong; Hebrews pairs it with keeping one another from being hardened by sin.

The hope Scripture gives is that God himself comforts the downcast, and he does it through people. Paul longed to visit Rome so that he and the church might be encouraged by each other's faith; he expected to receive as well as to give. You do not have to be strong to encourage someone. Often the word that helps most comes from a person who has needed the same word, and was given it.
deep.sit: Who in your life is carrying something heavy right now, and what one specific, true word could you say to them this week?

prayer.lead: The site's plain note calls Psalm 121 a blessing to carry out the door, and says you may pray it over someone you love as they set out. Pray it over the person you want to encourage, using their name.
prayer.text: The LORD is your keeper; the LORD is the shade on your right hand. The sun will not strike you by day, nor the moon by night. The LORD will guard you from all evil; He will preserve your soul. The LORD will watch over your coming and going, both now and forevermore.
